summary: Describes the interim NETRJS remote job entry service for the UCLA Campus Computing Network IBM 360 Model 91. Rand and UCLA/NMC had written user programs for it. It replaced RFC 88 and was expected to be superseded by a revised version. It was replaced by RFC 599.

eli5.summary: A mail-in window for sending big jobs to a powerful computer at UCLA. This is the instruction sheet for the temporary version.

subtitle: How a remote ARPANET site could submit batch jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 and collect the printed output.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users wanted to submit batch jobs to the IBM 360 Model 91 at the UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN) from their own hosts and get the results back.
tldr.mechanism: A user process acts as a virtual remote batch terminal. It signs on over a Telnet console connection, then opens separate data channels for a virtual card reader, printer and punch, carrying 8-bit transactions with a 72-bit header.
tldr.outcome: This is an interim protocol, expected to be superseded by a revised NETRJS. The text says it replaced RFC 88 and RFC 599 later obsoleted it.

today: RFC 189 obsoleted RFC 88 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 599. It was also updated by RFC 283. It describes an interim protocol and is not the current NETRJS specification.

sections.title: What NETRJS Does
sections.content:
NETRJS is the protocol for the remote job entry service to the 360 Model 91 at the UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN). It lets a user at a remote host reach CCN's RJS (Remote Job Service) subsystem, which also serves real remote batch terminals over direct lines.

Each active user process appears to RJS as a separate virtual remote batch terminal (VRBT), identified by an 8-character terminal id. A VRBT may have virtual card readers, printers and punches. Jobs sent through the virtual card reader as card images are spooled into the OS/360 MVT batch system, and print and punch output returns to the VRBT it came from unless the JCL names another destination.

The author says the interim protocol would be implemented as a production service before the end of July, with Rand and UCLA/NMC having already written user processes for it.

The cover note says the interim protocol would be superseded in a few months by a revised NETRJS with minor changes, bringing its data transfer protocol into conformity with the proposed Data Transfer Protocol in RFC 171. One planned change is moving the End-of-Data marker from X'FE' to X'B40F'.
sections.eli5: Your computer pretends to be a card-reading, printing terminal at UCLA. You feed in your job, and the printouts come back to you.

sections.title: Sessions and Channels
sections.content:
A session starts with the standard ICP from the user's socket U to socket 11 [sub] 10 (EBCDIC) or 13 [sub] 10 (ASCII) at host 1, IMP 1. The result is a duplex Telnet operator console connection. The user then enters SIGNON terminal-id; if the id is not recognized, RJS closes both console connections. For an ASCII VRBT, RJS translates input to EBCDIC and the printer stream back to ASCII, while the punch stream is always transparent.

Other channels sit at fixed offsets from the console socket S at CCN: card reader at S + 2, printer at S + 3 and punch at S + 5, with matching offsets from U at the user side. A session ends when the user closes all connections or enters SIGNOFF, after which RJS waits for current output streams to finish.
sections.eli5: You first sign in at the front desk. After that, separate doors at fixed spots handle the cards going in and the printouts coming out.

sections.title: Input, Output and the Data Transfer Format
sections.content:
A job stream is a series of card images of at most 80 characters, and jobs can be stacked, with a new job recognized by its JOB card. The user sends an End-of-Data transaction to start processing the last job. If NETRJS finds an error, such as a sequence number error, it aborts the channel and tells the user on the console that the job was discarded. Output arrives when RJS has something for an open printer or punch channel. The first record holds the job name, and printer records start with an ASA carriage control character.

Records travel in transactions preceded by a 72-bit header with a sequence number starting at 0 and a 32-bit length in bits. CCN's buffers are 880 bytes, so no transaction may exceed 880 bytes. Records are compressed (repeat counts for blanks or characters) or truncated, and the End-of-Data marker is X'FE'. The only error detection is the op code byte and the sequence number.
sections.eli5: Jobs go in as stacks of punched-card pictures, packed in numbered boxes no bigger than a set size. If a box goes missing or looks wrong, the whole delivery is stopped and redone.

sections.title: Console Commands
sections.content:
The remote operator console uses ASCII Telnet. Its commands control the terminal, jobs and output. STATUS lists jobs in the system for this VRBT, and MSG sends a message to the CCN operator or other RJS terminal. Output waits in an Active Queue or a Deferred Queue. DEFER and RESET move jobs between them, ROUTE redirects output, and ABORT cancels a job.

For output streams, BSP repeats the last page, RST restarts from the beginning of the data set or job, CAN skips output, and REPEAT sends extra copies. Console input lines over 133 characters are truncated.
sections.eli5: The console is like a remote control: ask what is happening to your jobs, pause printouts, send them somewhere else, or ask for a page again.
